$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=x(t)+2y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-2x(t)+5y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the system of linear differential equations above. The eigenvector $v=[2,\text{ }2]^{T}$ corresponds to the repeated eigenvalue $\lambda =3$ of the system's matrix $A.$ The vector $w=[-1,\text{ }0]^{T}$ is such that $(A-\lambda I)w=v.$ Select the correct options in the reasoning below.The general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}] & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t}+{c}_{2}([\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]t{e}^{3t}+[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{{field-1}}) \\  & ={c}_{1}{e}^{3t}{{field-2}}+{c}_{2}{e}^{3t}[\begin{aligned}2t-1 \\ 2t\end{aligned}],\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.\end{aligned}
$$

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to $v=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]$ has the equation 

$$
y={{field-3}}
$$

and the straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{3t}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]$
lie on that line. 

Since ${e}^{3t}\to $ 
{{field-4}} 
as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach 
{{field-5}}  
as $t\to \infty .$

Let's add the solutions to the phase space.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069697/assets/c993f6fc9eb12c0d8f60c420519a7db4a5cf78da9f0c24d0ade87b0a96590f59.png)

Now, consider solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{3t}[\begin{aligned}2t-1 \\ 2t\end{aligned}].$
When ${c}_{2}=4,$ we get the following curve:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=4(2t-1){e}^{3t} \\ y={{field-6}}\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the coordinates (rounded to two decimal places) of several points on the curve, we get the table below.

| $t$ | $-0.5$ | $0$ | $0.2$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $x$ | {{field-7}} | $-4$ | $-4.37$ |
| $y$ | {{field-8}} | $0$ | $2.92$ |

Let's add the solutions to the phase space.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069697/assets/6cc714f7f703eaebf31983882cbe988742ea47a9e280c7fbee1f44c877952b63.png)

The phase portrait of our system looks as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069697/assets/26ab713a8961e5668ee3663e0e5ac40ffbd6ea1dd02416ede0e2cbaaad4b63bf.png)

source.value:
Since we have a repeated eigenvalue $\lambda=-2$ (of multiplicity two) and only one corresponding eigenvector $\mathbf{v},$ the solution of the system is given by

$$
\mathbf{x}(t) = c_1\mathbf{v} e^{\lambda t}  + c_2 (\mathbf{v}  te^{\lambda t}  +  \mathbf{w}e^{\lambda t} \, ),
$$

where $\mathbf{w}$ is a solution to the equation $(A - \lambda I)\mathbf{w}= \mathbf{v}.$

In our case, 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069697/assets/15e5c3f06172ad8218375d20178b96a80de122300761fa4a615aca099d13c52a.png) 
Thus, the general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}] & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2t}+{c}_{2}([\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]t{e}^{-2t}+[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2t}) \\  & ={c}_{1}{e}^{-2t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}{e}^{-2t}[\begin{aligned}t \\ -t+1\end{aligned}],\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.\end{aligned}
$$

The line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069697/assets/daa87299ff267ce47cf44b06b218f533de30e780b12905d0e0a1888a50893dd0.png) has the equation 

$$
y= -x
$$

and the straight-line solutions of the form
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069697/assets/869e6bf67c0a5826b8d29130e8bf2107674508a103c4fb5a3d7d70ab78577090.png)
lie on that line. 

Since $e^{-2t} \to 0$ as $t \to \infty,$ these solutions approach the origin as $t \to \infty.$

Let's add the solutions to the phase space.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069697/assets/523dccf73169d02b6bdf4297e96ec84bcc6c43213cdd722000f3a987a534b218.png)

Now, consider solutions of the form
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069697/assets/4fc6300682b6e28d47e43802aba9427e29c606fc6c4f77edad874e7c0e4e2c01.png)
When $c_2=1,$ we get the following curve:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=t{e}^{-2t} \\ y=(-t+1){e}^{-2t}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Computing the coordinates (rounded to two decimal places) of several points on the curve, we get the table below.

| $t$ | $-0.5$ | $0$ | $0.5$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $x$ | $-1.36$ | $0$ | $0.18$ |
| $y$ | $4.08$ | $1$ | $0.18$ |

Let's add the solutions to the phase space.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069697/assets/dbf5a13ecd5e81c399204fd29d235e410fcb62274555cf3e5b32a383c1078d24.png)

The phase portrait of our system looks as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069697/assets/6c84cd04f3b037bee48d02d3183114e2668fbbd110bd44e9311e7ff454db8bac.png)

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069697/assets/7d16f04f098fc32370423b1b7adaa84c14b92291bde82672b65977b0498ec011.png)
